abstract: Obesity-associated adipose inflammation contributes to metabolic dysfunction, yet the mechanisms linking mitochondrial metabolism to macrophage efferocytosis remain incompletely understood. The mitochondrial dicarboxylate carrier (mDIC), encoded by SLC25A10, regulates adipocyte function, but its role in macrophages remains unclear. Here, we investigated how myeloid mDIC deficiency affects mitochondrial function, macrophage heterogeneity, and metabolic homeostasis during diet-induced obesity. We observed reduced mDIC protein expression in subcutaneous white adipose tissue from individuals with obesity, whereas palmitate increased mDIC expression in mouse and human macrophages. Myeloid mDIC deletion preserved mitochondrial respiration under palmitate stress. Single-cell RNA sequencing of adipose stromal vascular cells from high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice revealed an expanded efferocytosis-associated macrophage population and reduced proportions of inflammatory and lipid-associated macrophages. Consistently, mDIC-deficient macrophages exhibited increased Mertk expression and greater association with apoptotic cells. Pharmacological inhibition of mitochondrial ATP synthase or electron transport markedly suppressed apoptotic cell uptake, including the quenching-resistant fraction, without substantially affecting macrophage viability. In vivo, myeloid mDIC deletion attenuated HFD-induced weight gain, improved insulin sensitivity, and increased CD11c-CD206 adipose macrophage abundance, accompanied by elevated expression of alternative activation-associated markers. Together, these findings identify myeloid mDIC as an important regulator of macrophage mitochondrial function and adipose immune remodeling during obesity, suggesting a novel mechanism by which mitochondrial bioenergetics contribute to macrophage apoptotic-cell handling and metabolic homeostasis.
